final_proof:
The statement has an indexing defect if ℕ denotes {0,1,2,…}. Indeed, take V = ℝ, let v₀ = 1 and vₙ = 0 for every n ≥ 1, and take r = 1. For the directed set of finite subsets F ⊆ ℕ (ordered by inclusion), both the finite sum ∑_{n∈F} vₙ and the finite norm-sum ∑_{n∈F} ‖vₙ‖ are equal to 1 as soon as F contains 0. Thus the generalized sum is absolutely net convergent, with absolute sum 1. On the other hand, ∑_{n=1}^∞ vₙ is the zero series, whose absolute sum is 0, not 1. Hence, under the convention ℕ = {0,1,2,…}, (1) does not imply (2), and the claim as displayed is false. (If ℕ is defined to mean {1,2,3,…}, there is no mismatch and the displayed claim is true.)

The corrected statement is: the generalized sum and the series must use the same index set. Thus one may either replace the index set in (1) by ℕ₊ = {1,2,3,…}, or replace the lower limit in (2) by 0. We prove the first version; the proof of the second is identical after replacing {1,…,N} by {0,…,N}.

Put aₙ = ‖vₙ‖ ≥ 0. Let 𝔽 be the set of all finite subsets of ℕ₊, directed by inclusion, and define

A_F = ∑_{n∈F} aₙ  (F ∈ 𝔽),    s_N = ∑_{n=1}^N aₙ.

By definition, absolute net convergence of the generalized sum to r means A_F → r, while absolute convergence of the series to r means s_N → r.

First suppose A_F → r. The map N ↦ {1,…,N} is order-preserving and cofinal from ℕ₊ into 𝔽: for every finite F ∈ 𝔽, choosing N ≥ max F gives F ⊆ {1,…,N}. Consequently (s_N) is a subnet of (A_F). Every subnet of a convergent net has the same limit, so s_N → r. This proves (1) ⇒ (2).

Conversely, suppose s_N → r. Since every aₙ is nonnegative, (s_N) is increasing. For fixed N we have s_N ≤ s_M whenever M ≥ N; letting M tend to infinity gives s_N ≤ r. Let ε > 0. Choose N such that 0 ≤ r − s_N < ε, and set F₀ = {1,…,N}. If F ∈ 𝔽 and F ⊇ F₀, choose M ≥ max F. Nonnegativity then gives

s_N ≤ A_F ≤ s_M ≤ r.

It follows that |A_F − r| = r − A_F ≤ r − s_N < ε. This holds for every F ⊇ F₀, which is precisely A_F → r. Hence (2) ⇒ (1).

Finally, if the definitions of ‘absolutely convergent’ also explicitly require convergence of the corresponding V-valued sums, that requirement follows from the same estimates and completeness of V. Indeed, for m > n,

‖∑_{k=n+1}^m v_k‖ ≤ ∑_{k=n+1}^m ‖v_k‖ = s_m − s_n,

which tends to 0 as m,n → ∞; hence the vector partial sums are Cauchy and converge because V is Banach. Likewise the net of finite vector subsums is Cauchy: after choosing N with r − s_N < ε/2, any F,G ⊇ {1,…,N} satisfy

‖∑_{n∈F}vₙ − ∑_{n∈G}vₙ‖ ≤ ∑_{n∈F∖G}aₙ + ∑_{n∈G∖F}aₙ ≤ 2(r − s_N) < ε.

Thus it too converges in V. This completes the proof of the corrected equivalence, and it proves the original displayed equivalence whenever ℕ means the positive integers.
